items.title: America Can’t Afford an AI Recession
items.description: Over the past several days, as Donald Trump has flown across the country to rally Republican voters in contested midterm races, he has returned again and again to a version of the same point: “I had the greatest economy in the history of our country in my first term,” as the president told crowds in Michigan. “This term is going to blow it away.” To the extent Trump can claim the economy as a strength, what he’s mostly talking about is the biggest infrastructure build in American history. The five largest AI-data-center companies, including Amazon and Google, are on track to spend $900 billion on AI in 2026, roughly as much as they did in the previous three years combined. Just two AI chipmakers accounted for one-third of growth in corporate profits this past quarter, while as of September, AI stocks accounted for nearly half of growth in the S&P 500 in 2026. Depending on how you count, AI investments might already make up more than 8 percent of the nation’s GDP. [ Read: ] Welcome to the valley of pain Then there’s the rest of the economy, which is, if not struggling, at least confusing. AI has been pushing up the stock market for years, but the scale of financial expenditures is beginning to frighten investors, prompting a recent tumble. Gas and grocery prices are rising, while wages are largely flat or falling. There are tariffs and a miserable housing market. Unemployment is low, but at the same time, many Americans aren’t looking for work and job growth is slow. Consumer spending is strong, but that’s due in no small part to AI doubling the value of people’s stock portfolios since roughly the launch of ChatGPT. For years we’ve spoken of AI as a “boom,” describing explosive growth in one industry. It is more correct to speak of the entire market as the AI economy. Meanwhile, there’s real anxiety around the products these AI companies are selling. AI-powered hacks have brought about a cybersecurity apocalypse . OpenAI and Anthropic, the two companies whose futures the U.S. economy rests on, are losing control of their own agents and warning that these bots could end the world. The AI industry appears to be heading in two different directions—one financial, the other technological. Combined, their effect is to induce a sort of dependency: to bring about so much rapid change that AI becomes impossible for us to quit. The AI build-out was always big, but of late it has become gargantuan. Silicon Valley is committed to pushing as much money, human talent, electricity, concrete, and land toward AI as possible. The scope of the investment is staggering, estimated to be a bigger portion of GDP than the railroad boom and interstate highway system were, combined. Anthropic’s public offering next month could be the largest ever, perhaps valuing the company at $2 trillion. According to a recent Securities and Exchange Commission filing, Anthropic already has up to $807 billion in future contractual obligations for AI infrastructure to pay and expects “expenditures to increase significantly.” For reference, U.S. defense spending was $954 billion in 2025 . The biggest cloud companies, similarly, have nearly $3 trillion in contractual obligations already on the books, and will soon surpass $1 trillion in annual spending. Earnings reports last month showed that many of these companies—Meta, Google, Amazon—are already losing money because of their AI investments, which is stunning given that they all generate hundreds of billions of dollars a year in revenue. The role the AI industry has claimed for itself is in essence that of a central bank, managing the economy and issuing money to keep it afloat. The tremendous costs of data centers require the economy to run hot. AI firms need their customers to have money on hand in order to sustain meteoric revenue growth. But, according to at least one analysis , the AI industry’s cash-flow projections dwarf the far more modest ones of its biggest customers, raising the question of who’s going to fund AI’s continued development. Similarly, a robust stock market is necessary to attract more investors. And more wealth all around makes it easier for Meta, Google, and the like to issue debt to fund more data centers; this summer, foreign investors purchased more bonds from U.S. companies than from the federal government. So those same firms keep putting money into the flywheel: Nvidia, for instance, is dumping tens of billions of dollars into data centers used by distressed cloud companies that will, in turn, spend that money to buy Nvidia chips. It’s very possible the U.S. economy would be in a recession, or at least stagnant, without the AI boom. But it’s almost certain that there would be no AI build-out if the economy were to flail. Another way to think of the AI industry’s role in the broader economy is as a parasite, starving the rest of the organism. There are historic precedents for this: In 1959, for instance, oil companies in the Netherlands discovered enormous natural-gas reserves in the North Sea. The Dutch natural-gas industry grew rapidly—as did the nation’s GDP—but at the expense of other industries, including manufacturing, which withered. Today, in the U.S., profit margins are soaring at the biggest tech companies but flat for the rest of the S&P 500. Data-center construction is booming, but all other private construction is in free fall . The only source of private investment contributing to GDP growth is tech, according to an analysis by Pacific Investment Management Company. Meanwhile, the boom in demand for chips, natural gas, and construction materials driven by data-center build-outs is helping drive up inflation and make everyday life still more unaffordable. Silicon Valley is thriving, as are many broad macroeconomic indicators, but if you scratch beneath the surface, you’d find the finances of many Americans floundering. And what’s it all for? A large part of the reason for the step change in AI spending this year has been the rise of agents—programs, such as Claude Code and Muse, that write software and take complex actions on users’ behalf . Over the past few months, these products have caused chaos. Agents are being used by hospitals to charge more for health care and gaining unauthorized access to bank accounts. Hackers are breaching those hospitals, as well as governments, utilities, and financial instutions—recently pulling off perhaps the biggest cyberheist ever , draining billions from the crypto exchange Binance—and threatening the stability of the internet as we know it. That’s not to mention the ways the AI boom has, for years now, left classrooms a mess, driven up carbon emissions, and polluted the internet with slop. The strongest part of the American economy is also seemingly the most wasteful and destructive. The societal benefits of AI are largely either vague or delayed. A wave of AI-discovered drugs has yet to hit pharmacies. The technology has yet to solve climate change, as top executives including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have claimed it will do. Economy-wide data do not show clear signs of AI-driven productivity gains. The AI industry is conscious of the dissonance between their economic and technological ambitions and the mess their products are making. This fall, in an interview with The New York Times ’ Ezra Klein, Huang likened the cost of developing the technology to surgery: “They’ve got to cut you open to save you. They’ve got to inflict an enormous amount of pain and suffering on you so that they can save you. And so I think AI’s kind of like that.” In the meantime, thank Nvidia for your 401(k) doing very well. A year ago, there was a sense that the AI boom had put the American economy in a sort of “benevolent hostage situation.” Now the industry seems to be holding not just the American economy but our entire society hostage: Nvidia, Google, and the like had better succeed financially, or there go your savings. Anthropic and OpenAI had better succeed in their battle against AI-powered hacks, or there goes the internet. The technology had better be used to devise new carbon-free technologies, personal tutors for every kid, and widely available mental-health resources. There’s a perverse way in which even strident AI critics may be forced to cheer on some version of this industry: The only thing more destructive than the AI boom might be a crash.

items.title: Can You See What Holds This Painting Together?
items.description: Jackson Pollock became famous after an article ran in Life magazine under the headline, “Is He the Greatest Living Painter in the United States?” The headline, accompanied by indelible photos of the artist and his work, invited two types of responses: You must be kidding and If he is, wow—things are about to get interesting . That was August 1949. By the early ’60s, Pollock was no longer around, but modern art in America had indeed become interesting. Money was rolling in. Collectors competed for the latest groundbreaking work. The public’s interest was piqued. So Life commissioned an article on another artist, Roy Lichtenstein. The headline it ran under, with Lichtenstein’s approval, was: “Is He the Worst Artist in the U.S.?” Life published the profile in 1964, a couple years after Lichtenstein’s first exhibition of Pop-style paintings at Leo Castelli’s New York gallery. That show made a cause célѐbre of Lichtenstein. It included painted reproductions of a magnified comic-strip scene ( Blam ) and radically distilled, deadpan renderings of a washing machine, a turkey, an engagement ring, and a laughing cat (later acquired by Andy Warhol). Once the Life article was published, Lichtenstein’s prices shot up. Controversy fueled his fame. Some people, such as the critic Otto Hahn, praised his work for imbuing “monstrously tasteless imagery” with “tragic, anonymous grandeur.” Others thought him a copycat and questioned whether he was an artist at all. The Castelli show has been faithfully duplicated, down to the lighting fixtures and parquet floor, inside “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New,” an exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art. Organized by the Whitney curator Meg Onli and the artist Alex da Corte, it’s the first retrospective devoted to Lichtenstein in New York in 33 years. Today, Lichtenstein’s distinctive visual idiom—comic-book brevity given the high-art treatment—is as synonymous with postwar Pop art as Warhol’s soup cans and celebrity screen prints. His Ben Day–like dots and speech bubbles are copied onto bedsheets, handbags, Band-Aids, and billboards. The Whitney show is an opportunity to ask whether the paintings themselves hold up in the face of this 65-year storm of reproduction and commerce. Any answer is going to be moderated by irony, precisely because the paintings gained their original frisson by looking like commodities and copies. Lichtenstein’s zippy humor is suggested by his embrace of the Life article headline. It’s clear from other stories too. In 1965, for instance, the artist and his future wife, Dorothy Herzka, showed up at a Halloween party dressed as Warhol and Edie Sedgwick. It was a good gag—both visually (look at the photo and you could swear it was them) and conceptually: Warhol and Lichtenstein were by then the two leading figures of the growing Pop-art movement and well known for their interest in duplication. [ Read: Why is Warhol still so famous? ] Like Warhol, Lichtenstein was savvy about how, after Pollock, the currency of notoriety operated in America’s art world. While the Life profile was being prepared, he painted the hilarious Image Duplicator . It shows a cartoon villain—surely a coded self-portrait—in close-up, his evil blue eyes, blond eyebrows, and red mask overlaid by a speech bubble: WHAT ? WHY DID YOU ASK THAT ? WHAT DO YOU KNOW ABOUT MY IMAGE DUPLICATOR ? Lichtenstein was not just being droll. He was fascinated by the implications of duplication. In 1961, he made two near-identical portraits showing a generic man wearing a bow tie. He titled one Portrait of Allan Kaprow and the other Portrait of Ivan Karp . But in reality, Kaprow and Karp, both friends of Lichtenstein, looked nothing alike. What, he seemed to be asking, is gained when we duplicate or mechanically reproduce something, and what is lost? Jason Lowrie and Yvonne Tnt / BFA.com Installation view of “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” The Whitney show’s title comes from another peculiar exercise in duplication: a 1962 pencil drawing titled Like New . The work, for all its modesty, is at once funny and slyly philosophical, and a reminder that Lichtenstein was as much a conceptualist and minimalist as a Pop celebrant. Lichtenstein made Like New during his breakthrough years, when he rendered common objects—an electrical cord, a hot dog, a notebook, a tire—in a style borrowed from mass-media reproductions. (“I’m never drawing the object itself,” Lichtenstein explained. “I’m only drawing a depiction of the object—a kind of crystallized symbol of it.”) Like New shows two grids, side by side. The wall label says they represent window screens, but they’re really just pencil lines forming tight grids. The taut verticals and horizontals on the left are broken near the center, their loose ends turning wavy and stray, like the strings of a tennis racket smashed over a pole. The screen on the right has been restored to its immaculate, unified state—like new. Was Lichtenstein mocking America’s dream of repair? Was he questioning the ability of consumer society to “make it new”—to restore order and harmony and fix what was broken? These questions feel too big for such a humble work. The Second World War, though, was not so far in the past. Lichtenstein, who had been drafted into the Army in 1943 and deployed to Europe, was discharged in 1946. Fifteen years later, the economy was booming and households were filling with products. But the new consumerism, Lichtenstein seemed to suggest, was a fragile scrim over a moral and spiritual void. Decades earlier, between the world wars, the German poet Rainer Maria Rilke had lamented to a friend the loss of a depth of meaning that he associated with handmade objects passed down from one generation to the next, each with its own history of use, care, and repair. “Now, from America,” he complained , “empty indifferent things are pouring across, sham things, dummy life.” Lichtenstein, almost 40 years later, was conscious not just of objects pouring out of factories but also of the way that people’s desire for such objects was manufactured by advertising. He wanted to portray, he said, “the lack of sensibility, the lack of refinement, the kind of immediate, not contemplative answer that society keeps giving us.” Portraying is crucially different from critiquing: Lichtenstein’s paintings deliberately lacked signs of “sensibility.” They were as vacant and affectless as a showroom washing machine. But they may be more contemplative than they appear. Lichtenstein, who loved to read Scientific American , was fascinated by systems of visual perception. As a student at Ohio State University, he had been heavily influenced by Hoyt Sherman, a fine-arts professor who taught classes in perceptual training. (Along with co-curating the show, Da Corte, one of the most compelling artists working today, has created a short film about Sherman, casting himself as the professor, which is screening in the show’s opening gallery.) The secret of visual perception, for Sherman, had nothing to do with the thing you were looking at. Instead, as Lichtenstein explained, it was about “building a unified pattern of seeing.” To develop perceptual skills, Sherman would place students in a dark room that he called a “flash lab.” He would abruptly turn the lights on and off and, after the room returned to darkness, make students draw what they had seen. He was teaching them to find unities, to register what it is that holds the visual field together. [ Read: The artist who ripped up the rules of drawing ] Outside of the flash lab, the surest way for an artist to achieve unity on paper or canvas is to convert the visual field into units of, for instance, cross-hatching, dashes, or dots. But when you convert visual phenomena into a system of fungible units, something is gained and something lost. The world becomes, as Da Corte suggests in the exhibition catalog, like a sponge, or like Swiss cheese: conceptually unified but slightly less substantial than it had been. Is anything about this sounding familiar? Jason Lowrie and Yvonne Tnt / BFA.com Installation view of “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” In 1966, Lichtenstein compared his dots to digital technologies, suggesting that his paintings possessed a “data information quality.” Two years later, he began work on a series of five panels inspired by Claude Monet’s more than two dozen paintings of Rouen Cathedral from the early 1890s. Lichtenstein’s gambit was to reduce Monet’s thickly encrusted, opalescent paint to two-color combinations of mechanical dots. The resulting patterns, up close, seem abstract and insubstantial. At a distance, however, they resolve, like Monet’s paintings, into the cathedral facades. Cezanne famously said of Monet that he was “only an eye—but, my God, what an eye.” What Sherman and then Lichtenstein understood was that we are never “only an eye.” Eyes are attached to brains and bodies, which continually mediate raw perception. (When we open our eyes, the brain’s first task is to overturn a law of optics: The flow of images coming in through the eyes is upside down.) We see the world, moreover, through a changing set of conventions. Human technologies—from oil paint and printmaking to photography and the computer—all establish new conventions that affect how we perceive the world. These conventions can be useful, even delightful; but they act like veils between us and reality, often hardening into clichés, tired from overuse. Modernism’s project was to see the world afresh by disrupting convention and stripping away clichés. As technologies advanced, modern artists sensed something broken about our connection to reality. They wanted to establish less secondhand ways of perceiving. Many of their attempts were concerned with fixing what was broken and reestablishing a sense of spiritual wholeness. [ Read: The marriage that captures a high point of American art ] Lichtenstein’s interest in Monet was far from arbitrary. The Impressionists—the first modernists—had disrupted traditional pictorial conventions by dispensing with drawing, tone, narrative, and expression and funneling all the many facets of perception through a single lens: colored light. This was how they established their new, reparative unity. After them, Georges Seurat and his pointillist followers unified their pictures by converting Impressionist light into a scientific system of atomized color relations. Piet Mondrian—another modernist Lichtenstein thought hard about—took this principle further. He converted the visible world into a grid, a binary system of rectilinear divisions of space and primary colors. Lichtenstein shared the early-modernist impulse to “make it new.” But he was working in an era marked by rampant consumerism and accelerating technologies of reproduction. These technologies had long prehistories, going back to intaglio and halftone printing, which built up images with sophisticated patterns of dots, and then to such innovations as the Ben Day dot system, invented in 1879 by Benjamin Henry Day Jr., and later adapted by Lichtenstein. Another technology, the Xerox machine, was released in 1959. When, two years later, Disney made One Hundred and One Dalmatians , this new image duplicator helped replicate animators’ drawings, and soon, according to Da Corte, scores had lost their jobs. Handmade drawing was replaced by mechanical reproduction. Of course, one way to contend with technology’s veils is to tear them down. Pablo Picasso was thinking along these lines when he described his pictures as “a sum of destructions.” Another way is simply to draw attention to them—perhaps by repeating them over and over, as when you repeat a word until it becomes absurd or takes on an entirely different meaning. Lichtenstein’s project was more in the second category. Through sustained visual panache and persistent, peppy wit, he helped mid-century America see itself. There’s a reason his work slides happily into the key of today: The conventions and technologies governing our reality have only become more fungible, the answers to our questions more standardized and ironed out. If his proliferating dots create a scrim of reality analogous to Swiss cheese, he sensitizes us to the holes—perhaps with what Elias Canetti had in mind when he wrote: “The hopeful things in any system are the things that have been left out.”

items.title: Recettes incertaines, exécution fragile : les alertes du PNCD 2026-2030
items.description: Le Plan national de croissance et de développement vise une croissance moyenne de 6,5 % entre 2026 et 2030. Mais le document prévient lui-même : les recettes attendues pourraient manquer et les projets prendre du retard. Sans une meilleure gestion publique, les résultats économiques annoncés deviendraient «irréalisables». Le PNCD 2026-2030 avertit : annoncer les milliards ne construit pas le pays. Encore faut-il bien les utiliser. © GabonReview (montage) Le Gabon veut accélérer son développement. Pour y parvenir, le Plan national de croissance et de développement (PNCD) 2026-2030 mise notamment sur l’énergie, les infrastructures et les activités hors pétrole. Mais ce document du ministère de la Planification et de la Prospective ne présente pas seulement des objectifs. Il explique aussi ce qui pourrait empêcher de les atteindre. Aux pages 161 et 162, les auteurs identifient plusieurs difficultés : l’État pourrait percevoir moins d’argent que prévu, les projets pourraient être mal exécutés et les investissements produire des résultats insuffisants. Ces avertissements permettent de comprendre les conditions nécessaires à la réussite du plan. L’argent attendu pourrait manquer Le premier risque concerne les recettes de l’État. Le PNCD juge élevé le risque que les sommes prévues dans la loi de finances 2026 ne soient pas effectivement encaissées. Cela pourrait réduire les moyens disponibles pour financer les investissements publics. Le plan prévoit un déficit budgétaire de 6 % du produit intérieur brut (PIB) en 2026. Cela signifie que l’État dépenserait davantage qu’il ne percevrait, avec un écart équivalant à 6 % de la richesse produite dans le pays en une année. L’objectif est de ramener ce déficit sous 3 % à partir de 2029. Pour y arriver, le Gabon devra notamment augmenter ses recettes hors pétrole et maîtriser ses dépenses de fonctionnement. Si les rentrées d’argent restent inférieures aux prévisions ou si les dépenses augmentent trop, l’étude prévient que la dette pourrait dépasser le niveau attendu. Des budgets à transformer en réalisations Trouver l’argent ne suffit pas. Encore faut-il réussir à réaliser les projets. Selon le PNCD, le taux d’exécution du Programme d’investissements publics se situe historiquement autour de 50 %. Le plan veut le porter au-delà de 90 %. Cet objectif demande de mieux préparer les projets, de choisir ceux qui sont les plus utiles et d’en suivre sérieusement l’avancement. Le document insiste donc sur la gouvernance, c’est-à-dire la manière dont les décisions sont prises, les moyens utilisés et les résultats contrôlés. Son avertissement est direct : « Si la gouvernance ne s’améliore pas, l’ensemble du cadre macro-économique projeté devient irréalisable .» En termes simples, les résultats économiques prévus ne pourront pas être atteints sans une meilleure gestion. Les conséquences dépasseraient les seuls projets de l’État. D’après le document, une gestion publique insuffisante rend aussi le pays moins attractif pour les investisseurs privés et les partenaires susceptibles de financer son développement. Investir davantage, mais surtout investir mieux Le PNCD souligne un autre risque : dépenser plus sans obtenir suffisamment de résultats. Si les investissements ne permettent pas de produire davantage et de développer les activités économiques, les recettes fiscales attendues pourraient être plus faibles. L’État aurait alors davantage de difficultés à financer la suite du programme. L’énergie et les infrastructures jouent ici un rôle essentiel. Les entreprises ont besoin d’électricité et de moyens de transport pour fonctionner. Des retards dans ces secteurs pourraient donc ralentir de nombreuses autres activités. Le document ne dit pas que le plan échouera. Il précise ce qui doit changer pour qu’il réussisse. Les résultats dépendront de l’argent réellement mobilisé, de la qualité des projets retenus et de la capacité à les mener jusqu’au bout. L’article Recettes incertaines, exécution fragile : les alertes du PNCD 2026-2030 est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Sudanese Journalists’ Syndicate documents 673 violations and calls for end to impunity
items.description: The Sudanese Journalists’ Syndicate has documented 673 violations against journalists since the outbreak of war in Sudan on 15 April 2023, including 34 killings, 116 cases of arbitrary arrest, detention, and enforced disappearance, and 120 cases of threats and hate speech. In a statement marking the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists , the syndicate’s Freedom Secretariat highlighted the deteriorating security and professional conditions facing journalists in Sudan since the conflict began. Journalist Muammar Ibrahim has been detained by the Rapid Support Forces for over a year (Photo: Supplied) The syndicate says threats against journalists have taken increasingly dangerous forms. By the end of June 2026, it had documented 673 violations, including the killing of 34 male and female journalists, 116 cases of arrest, arbitrary detention, and enforced disappearance, 120 cases of threats and hate speech, and 34 incidents of direct targeting and gunfire. Other violations included physical assaults, looting, institutional abuses, and cross-border violations. Graphic: RD The Freedom Secretariat expressed particular concern over the cases of five journalists who have been subjected to enforced disappearance. They are Ashraf El Habr, in areas controlled by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF); Musab El Hadi, whose captors remain unknown; and Mustafa Fadl El Mawla, Magdi Youssef El Zein and Mohamed Hussein Shalabi, in areas controlled by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The syndicate also documented arbitrary arrests involving Adam Ishaq Manan and Maamar Ibrahim. It said that complete information was unavailable about detainees held in areas under SAF control, underscoring the urgent need to establish their whereabouts and secure their immediate release. 64 legal cases documented On legal proceedings against journalists, the syndicate revealed that it had documented 64 cases of prosecution during the war. Graphic: RD These included complaints filed under the Cybercrime Act against 47 journalists and media organisations in a single instance, following which 18 journalists were declared wanted fugitives. The syndicate warned about recent amendments to the Cybercrime Act and Article 51/A of the 1991 Criminal Act, which brought electronic and media publishing within the scope of the legislation. It also raised concerns about the establishment of a national mechanism to combat cybercrime in the absence of stronger safeguards for freedom of expression. The Freedom Secretariat called for independent and transparent investigations into crimes targeting journalists and for those responsible to be held accountable. It also demanded the repeal of restrictive legal provisions that curtail freedom of expression and the press, and an end to the use of criminal laws and emergency powers as instruments of repression. The Secretariat further called for full protection for the journalistic community and guaranteed access to information, stressing that combating impunity is fundamental to safeguarding press freedom and society’s right to know. Graphic: RD ‘Women journalists’ voices and pens deserve protection ‘ As reported by Radio Dabanga today, Sudan’s Women Journalists Network has warned of escalating violations and crimes against journalists in Sudan, particularly women, and a growing culture of impunity amid the continuing war, widespread availability of weapons, proliferation of armed militias, and weakening state institutions. In a report issued to mark International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists , the network called for an end to the war, the disarmament of militias, and investigations into crimes and violations committed against journalists, with those responsible held accountable and justice and redress secured for victims and survivors. #Endimpunity Share article The post Sudanese Journalists’ Syndicate documents 673 violations and calls for end to impunity appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .

items.title: HKEX extends overnight derivatives trading as Hong Kong chases global market flow
items.description: Bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) is taking a further step towards round-the-clock trading by pushing back the closing bell for its after-hours derivatives market by 75 minutes from next year, according to a statement released on Monday. The derivatives After-Hours Trading (AHT) session would extend to 4.15am from 3am, Hong Kong time, starting in March 2027, subject to regulatory approval and system readiness, according to HKEX. items.title: Kati Dral : le préfet présente les condoléances aux familles des trois enfants tués dans un accident
items.description: Trois enfants, dont deux membres d’une même famille, ont perdu la vie le lundi 19 octobre 2026, après avoir été percutés par un camion transportant du bétail alors qu’ils se rendaient à l’école. Le drame a profondément bouleversé les habitants des logements sociaux de Kati Dral.

items.title: Consumer inflation falls to 9.6pc in Oct from 10.3pc in Sept
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Consumer inflation eased to 9.6 per cent in October from 10.3pc a month earlier , mainly due to a slight slowdown in perishable food products, the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics said on Monday. The slowdown in the inflation rate for the second consecutive month, measured by the Consumer Price Index, reversed the sharp increase recorded in August , when higher food and energy prices pushed the annual rate to 11.1pc from 9.2pc in July. The easing was recorded in both places, in rural areas where inflation fell to 9.5pc from 10.1pc, while urban inflation edged down to 9.8pc from 10.5pc. The October reading was also within the Ministry of Finance’s projection of 9.5pc to 10.5pc for the month in its Monthly Economic Update and Outlook for October . According to the finance ministry, easing headline inflation offers some relief, while improved crop supplies can help ease food price pressures. However, despite the decline in the annual rate, prices rose 1.1pc month-on-month in October. The annual inflation rate was 6.2pc in October last year. The average inflation between July and October stood at 10.05pc compared with 4.79pc over the corresponding period last year. The easing was largely driven by perishable food prices. Food inflation dropped to 7.8pc in urban areas in October from 8.1pc in September. The decline was much sharper in rural areas, where food inflation fell to 7.1pc from 7.7pc a month earlier. However, non-food inflation moved in the opposite direction, indicating continued pressure on household expenses. Urban non-food inflation decelerated to 10.6pc from 11.5pc in September, while rural non-food inflation fell to 12.3pc from 13.1pc. The latest data shows that the composition of inflation shifted in October. While food inflation slowed sharply, electricity and transport costs continued to rise. Electricity charges increased by 8.50pc from the previous month, while transport prices rose by 30.39pc in urban areas. At the national level, transport costs increased by 1.79pc during October from the previous month and were 28.61pc higher than in the same month last year. Housing, water, electricity, gas and fuels increased by 0.25pc during the month and by 11.03pc on an annual basis. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, also eased slightly. It stood at 7.8pc in urban areas in October, compared with 8.6pc in September, while the rural rate declined to 7.1pc from 8.1pc.

items.title: Máxima presión para el cese del presidente de Adif a horas de la comparecencia de Puente en el Congreso
items.description: “Toda la casa [por el gestor de la infraestructura ferroviaria Adif] está tensionada muy por encima de sus posibilidades en busca de respuestas al accidente de Urda , cuando aún no hemos salido del estado de shock , y manteniendo la operativa en la red de alta velocidad y en la convencional”. El diagnóstico de situación crítica es de un alto directivo de Adif que reclama el anonimato antes de una breve conversación. Lejos de parar máquinas para analizar lo sucedido en Urda (Toledo), el ritmo frenético diario debe continuar en los centros de control . Pero son horas decisivas para el curso de la investigación del siniestro que el pasado miércoles 28 de octubre costó la vida a 69 personas en la línea de altas prestaciones Madrid-Sevilla. El presidente de Adif, Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña, tiene toda la presión sobre los hombros, al igual que todo su comité ejecutivo. El cargo, afirman fuentes internas, está a disposición del ministro de Transportes desde el primer minuto. Y el de Óscar Puente , en manos del presidente del Gobierno. El cese de Marco de la Peña, antes o junto al de Puente, es un clamor entre los grupos de la oposición, también entre aliados del Grupo Socialista en el Congreso. Puente y Marco de la Peña, que comparecieron juntos en rueda de prensa el pasado viernes, se comprometieron en enero a trabajar para que un suceso como el de Adamuz (Córdoba), en la misma línea Madrid-Sevilla, no se repitiera . items.title: Clôture du Festival de la Grenade de Testour
items.description: La 10 e édition du Festival de la grenade de Testour (gouvernorat de Béja), qui s’est tenue du 27 octobre au 1er novembre 2026, a vu la participation d’environ 250 artisans et le marché de cette ville agricole du nord-ouest tunisien a connu une activité commerciale intense Pendant six jours, les habitants et les visiteurs ont eu droit à une forte animation culturelle et artistique autour de ce fruit emblématique de la région. Dans une déclaration à Diwan FM , Mouna Arfaoui, la directrice de l’association organisatrice, a avancé le chiffre d’un million de visiteurs, qui nous semble cependant quelque peu exagéré. Il y a eu des points de vente directe de grenades (du producteur au consommateur), ainsi que des séminaires visant à valoriser cette richesse agricole et à faire connaître ses spécificités, a-t-elle ajouté, en faisant part de sa volonté de donner au festival une dimension internationale afin d’impulser l’activité touristique dans cette ville fondée au Moyen-Âge par les Morisques Andalous chassés d’Espagne par la Reconquista chrétienne. Rappelons de la production tunisienne de grenades est estimée à 98 000 tonnes pour la saison 2026, ce qui représente une hausse de 8 % par rapport à la saison précédente (91 000 tonnes). Ce fruit est produit dans deux régions principales: Gabès, dans le sud-est, connue pour sa variété Gapsi protégée par une AOC, et Testour, pôle historique célèbre pour son Festival des grenades et ses certifications biologiques Ecocert . I. B. L’article Clôture du Festival de la Grenade de Testour est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .
